title: The Decades Progress on Code-Switching Research in NLP: A Systematic Survey on Trends and Challenges
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2023
problem_statement: A systematic investigation into decades of code-switching (CSW) research in natural language and speech processing to understand historical progress from linguistic theories to pre-trained neural language models, identify task and language coverage imbalances, evaluate dataset accessibility and attrition issues, and conceptualize open research challenges and future directions.
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Speech Processing, Code-Switching (CSW), Multilingual Language Modeling, Computational Linguistics
theoretical_framework: Grammatical and linguistic constraint theories of bilingual code-switching, including Poplack's Equivalence Constraint (1980), Myers-Scotton's Matrix-Embedded Language Framework (MLF) (1997, 2005), and Belazi et al.'s Functional Head Constraint (1994), alongside cognitive theories of multilingual competence and cross-lingual representation alignment.
methodology: Systematic literature survey and manual multi-annotator taxonomy coding analyzing over 400 papers published in the ACL Anthology (crawled up to October 2022) and ISCA proceedings using 14 code-switching search keywords. Three annotators categorized publications across language varieties (bilingual, trilingual, 4+; regional groups), publication venues, paper contribution genres, dataset sources/modalities, computational methodologies (rule-based/linguistic constraints, statistical methods, neural sequence models, pre-trained language models), and text/speech downstream tasks.
key_findings: The vast majority of code-switching NLP research is bilingual with English as one of the pair (particularly South Asian languages like Hindi, Tamil, Malayalam, as well as Spanish and Chinese), while non-English pairs, Middle Eastern languages, and multilingual switching (trilingual or 4+) remain substantially under-represented.

Language identification and sentiment analysis dominate ACL text-based code-switching research, whereas ASR and TTS dominate ISCA speech processing publications, demonstrating ongoing fragmentation between the speech and text processing research communities.

Social media text and recorded conversational speech constitute the primary data sources, but over 60% of surveyed corpora are private/closed, and social media datasets suffer from significant data attrition due to URL-only sharing policies and deleted posts.

The methodological paradigm has shifted from rule-based linguistic constraints (Poplack's equivalence constraint, MLF, functional head constraint) and statistical models (CRF, SVM, HMM) to neural sequence architectures (RNN/LSTM) and pre-trained multilingual language models (mBERT, XLM-R).

While pre-trained multilingual language models enable end-to-end task performance without manual linguistic rules, they lack interpretability regarding failure modes and face catastrophic forgetting/language attrition when fine-tuned on mixed-language inputs.
scope_and_delimitations: The survey systematically indexes academic literature on code-switching published in open proceedings of the ACL Anthology (up to October 2022) and ISCA conferences, supplemented by curated public research repositories.
The scope covers both written natural language processing and spoken speech processing modalities across token-level, sequence-level, and generative tasks.

The analysis excludes papers published after October 2022 and excludes fine-grained categorization of code-switching types (such as intra-sentential versus inter-sentential switching) due to lack of reporting in source literature.
The survey is non-empirical and synthesizes findings and statistics across literature without running new experimental benchmarks or retraining models.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: The numbers in this survey are limited to papers published in the ACL Anthology and ISCA Proceedings. However, we also included papers as related work from other resources if they are publicly available and accessible. In addition, the category in the survey does not include the code-switching type (i.e., intra-sentential, inter-sentential, etc.) since some papers do not provide such information.
limitations.summary: The quantitative review is delimited to publications indexed in the ACL Anthology and ISCA proceedings (excluding broader journals and post-October 2022 literature), and does not categorize fine-grained linguistic switching types (such as intra-sentential vs. inter-sentential switching) because many surveyed papers omit these structural details.

generalizability_gap: Code-switching research and resources are heavily skewed toward a few high-resource bilingual pairs involving English (Hindi-English, Spanish-English, Chinese-English). Geographic varieties, regional dialects, underrepresented indigenous languages, non-English mixed pairs, and complex multilingual interactions (trilingual and 4+ languages) remain severely understudied and lack generalizable models.
methodological_gap: Pre-trained multilingual models lack interpretability in code-switched contexts, suffer from catastrophic forgetting and cross-lingual representation degradation, and remain under-evaluated for scaling laws and compute-performance trade-offs. Furthermore, evaluation methods for generative code-switched text rely heavily on subjective human evaluation, lacking automated metrics that reliably align with human judgments of fidelity, style mimicry, and discourse naturalness.
future_work: Broadening language scope to under-represented code-switching styles, regional dialects, and non-English/multilingual (>2 languages) language combinations.
Developing open, accessible, and ecologically valid written code-switched corpora that avoid data attrition issues associated with social media APIs.
Investigating model scaling laws, compute-performance trade-offs, and zero-shot/few-shot prompt and instruction tuning with large multilingual foundation models on code-switched tasks.
Integrating code-switching evaluation into standardized cross-lingual benchmarks (e.g., XTREME-R, XGLUE) to assess model robustness and continual learning against catastrophic forgetting.
Creating complex reasoning and comprehension benchmarks for code-switched text, including natural language inference, coreference resolution, and question answering.
Developing code-switching conversational dialogue agents and generative models with automated evaluation metrics aligned with human judgments of quality, style, and naturalness.
